title: Contagion Live: A Doctor's Mission to Close the Hepatitis D Testing Gap
summary: For years, patients with hepatitis B were doing everything right, and still getting sicker. Charles M. Walworth, M.D., associate vice president of medical affairs and education and co-discipline director for molecular infectious diseases at Labcorp, joined the Contagion Live podcast "From Pathogen to Infectious Disease Diagnosis" to explain why, and what Labcorp is doing about it.
body_markdown:
For years, patients with hepatitis B were doing everything right, and still getting sicker. Charles M. Walworth, M.D., associate vice president of medical affairs and education and co-discipline director for molecular infectious diseases at Labcorp, joined the *Contagion Live* podcast "From Pathogen to Infectious Disease Diagnosis" to explain why, and what Labcorp is doing about it.


**Key takeaway:** Labcorp's new reflex test automatically checks hepatitis B patients for hepatitis D, a dangerous co-infection that has been overlooked for decades.


**Why it matters:** Walworth recalled treating hepatitis B patients more than 15 years ago who did everything right. "They stopped drinking alcohol. They stopped injecting drugs. They stopped taking toxic medications. Yet they seemed to progress more rapidly than they should have," he said. "There was no opportunity for hepatitis D testing back then… And I think to myself, how many of them could have been co-infected?"


Hepatitis D is the most severe form of viral hepatitis, yet fewer than 20% of U.S. hepatitis B patients are ever screened for it, even though an estimated 70,000 to 150,000 Americans live with active infection. The FDA's approval of the first hepatitis D treatment, bulevirtide-gmod (Hepcludex), in May 2026 made diagnosing the disease more important than ever. Labcorp responded with a reflex test that automatically checks the same blood sample for hepatitis D whenever hepatitis B is detected—no extra visit, no second blood draw.


The approach mirrors the hepatitis C testing model that helped scale hepatitis C diagnosis. Walworth and colleagues reviewed more than 38 million hepatitis C specimens from 2018 to 2024, published in[Clinical Infectious Diseases](https://academic.oup.com/cid/article-abstract/82/6/988/8643933?login=false) . Now Labcorp is applying that same proven playbook to a virus hiding in plain sight.


**Listen to the full podcast on**[Contagion Live.](https://www.contagionlive.com/view/from-pathogen-to-infectious-disease-diagnosis-reflex-testing-targets-hepatitis-d-gap)
